Chapter 6: The Scandal of Grace—When Love Offends Expectations.
You know, there comes a point in every real journey of faith when grace just feels... almost too much. It’s wild, isn’t it? The idea that love could actually be given—freely, without limits—even to the folks who seem like they deserve it least. It can feel kind of unsettling. Maybe even a little offensive.
I mean, deep down, haven’t you ever wondered—shouldn’t there be a line somewhere? Shouldn’t there be a point where someone’s just gone too far?
Picture this: a man who’s spent years making mistake after mistake. He’s burned bridges, let down everyone who ever cared, and now, he’s pretty sure forgiveness is for other people—not for him. One day, he drags himself into a small gathering, not because he expects anything, but because he’s run out of options. He braces for cold stares or maybe polite distance.
But what he finds? It’s warmth. It’s genuine welcome. Nobody asks for an explanation. Nobody demands an apology. They just make space for him, as if he belongs. And honestly, it throws him off. He’s never encountered a kind of love that doesn’t keep score.
Most of us, whether we admit it or not, keep our own secret scorecards. We’re always tallying up the wins and losses, measuring ourselves against everyone else. So, when someone says that God’s love actually wipes away the whole ledger—no conditions, no loopholes—it almost feels reckless.
But that’s what makes grace a scandal. It refuses to play by the rules of fairness. It’s not a prize you earn—it’s a gift you receive.
A lot of people get caught in this cycle of trying to earn their place. If I just do enough, maybe then I’ll finally be accepted. But grace steps in and interrupts all that striving. It says, “You’re loved first—not as a reward, but as your starting point.”
It’s usually the ones who’ve got nothing left to offer who end up receiving the most.
There’s something quietly revolutionary that happens when you stop trying to deserve love and just let yourself receive it. Those old walls of shame and self-condemnation? They start to fall away. Your heart softens a bit. The journey of faith shifts—from trying to prove you’re enough, to simply living in the freedom of being loved. No matter what.
